Here Am I; Send Me
HEER am EYE; SEND mee
n. phr. (Isaiah's answer in the temple vision, after his lips were touched)
Hebrew hinneni shelacheni — hinneni, behold me, the margin's own reading; shalach in the imperative with the first-person suffix, send me; the same hinneni answers God in the mouths of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Jacob.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, hears the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy, and cries out that he is undone, a man of unclean lips. A seraph then takes a live coal from the altar and touches his mouth, declaring his iniquity taken away and his sin purged. Only then comes the question and the answer: “Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.” The order of the chapter is the doctrine. Vision of God's holiness, conviction of sin, atonement applied from the altar, and only after that the call and the volunteering. A man who has not seen the thrice-holy God has nothing to say in that room, and a man whose lips are unclean cannot be sent until the coal has touched them. Notice also what Isaiah was sent to: the commission immediately following is to a people whose heart is made fat and whose ears are heavy, a ministry of preaching that would mostly not be received, and he accepted it. The phrase is therefore the opposite of an eager volunteer's slogan. It is the answer of a pardoned man who has learned who God is, and who says yes before he is told the terms.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Send, to cause to go or be carried; to commission and dispatch. Here, in this place; at this point. Here am I; send me, Isaiah 6:8, the prophet's answer after the coal from the altar had touched his lips.

Send, to cause to go or be carried; to commission and dispatch on an errand.

Here, in this place; present; at hand — the margin reads ‘behold me’.

Hebrew hinneni, behold me; the standing answer of a servant to God's call.

Hebrew shalach, to send; here imperative with the first-person suffix.

Follows the live coal from the altar and the purging of sin, Isaiah 6:6-7.

Key Scripture

Isa 6:8 — "Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me."

Isa 6:5 — "Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts."

Isa 6:3 — "And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory."

Rom 10:15 — "And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

Modern Corruption

The words are detached from the chapter and used as a missions-conference slogan of willingness, with the vision, the conviction, the altar coal, and the hard commission all left out.

expand to see more

Printed on banners and sung in choruses, the phrase now most often expresses raw availability — a willing heart offering itself. Isaiah's willingness is the fifth thing in the chapter, not the first. Before he says it he has seen the Lord's train fill the temple, heard the holy cry that shook the posts of the door, pronounced himself undone, and had his mouth touched with fire from the altar. Willingness without those is enthusiasm, and the church has sent out a great many enthusiastic men who had never been undone. The call to ministry in Scripture always runs through the holiness of God and the purging of the called man's sin.

The second omission is the commission itself. The very next verses tell Isaiah to preach to a people who will hear and not understand, and he asks how long, and is told until the cities are wasted. The modern use of his words implies an expectation of visible success, which is precisely what his own sending did not include. The principle to recover is that the measure of a sent man is faithfulness and not reception. He goes because the Lord has asked who will go, and he keeps going when the hearts are fat and the ears are heavy, as Isaiah did for a lifetime and as the apostles did after him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hinneni, behold me, the servant's answer used by Abraham, Jacob, Moses and Samuel; shalach, to send — spoken only after the altar coal had purged his lips.

Hebrew hinneni, behold me; the margin's reading of ‘Here am I’.

Hebrew shalach, to send or commission, imperative with first-person suffix.

Preceded by the thrice-holy cry of the seraphim, Isaiah 6:3.

Preceded by the live coal from the altar and sin purged, Isaiah 6:6-7.

Followed by a commission to unhearing ears, Isaiah 6:9-11.
